phishingSpot.title: Spot the spoof markers
phishingSpot.subtitle: Find seven spoof cues on this Bank of America look-alike email — click where each risk hides.
phishingSpot.instructions: Each correct tap matches one of the seven clues we teach (sender, branding, greeting, typos, urgency, link, sign-off). Wrong clicks show a hint.
phishingSpot.miss: That is not one of the seven spoof clues — try another area of the email.
phishingSpot.complete: You found every phishing indicator on this screenshot.
phishingSpot.missedSectionSubtitle: Highlighted in amber on the image above.
phishingSpot.imageAlt: Screenshot of a phishing email pretending to be from Bank of America.

spots.title: Fraudulent but similar domain name for sender
spots.detail: The From address uses ameribank7.com — a look-alike domain, not bankofamerica.com or another official bank host.

spots.title: Incorrect branding
spots.detail: Look at the institution name beside the logo — generic icons and imperfect typography beside “Bank of America” deserve extra scrutiny.

spots.title: Generic information
spots.detail: Dear account holder avoids using your real name — typical when scammers send one message to many recipients.

spots.title: Spelling errors
spots.detail: divice instead of device is a typo legitimate banks rarely leave in automated security notices.

spots.title: Sense of urgency
spots.detail: Claims such as four mystery transactions are meant to scare you into acting before you verify the alert.

spots.title: Fake link
spots.detail: The password-reset URL points to ameribank7.com — an attacker-controlled site meant to steal credentials, not the bank's real domain.

spots.title: Incorrect name
spots.detail: Bank America omits the word of compared with Bank of America used above — a subtle branding slip common in forgeries.
